claims.text: A controlled heat treatment can induce enhanced short-range ordering among chromium and other alloying elements in stainless steel without changing its bulk composition.
Short-range ordering promotes formation of a more continuous and protective chromium-oxide passive film.
A more continuous chromium-oxide passive film reduces localized corrosion.
Conventionally processed stainless steel has a comparatively random distribution of Cr, Ni, and Mo.
The proposed heat treatment produces nanoscale ordered domains or clusters enriched in chromium and possibly synergistic alloying elements.
Chromium-enriched ordered domains act as uniformly distributed nucleation sites for a stable protective chromium-oxide film.
Short-range ordering reduces the occurrence of chromium-deficient regions in stainless steel.
Reducing chromium-deficient regions produces a more uniform passivation layer.
A more uniform passivation layer suppresses pitting by retaining barrier integrity under corrosive attack.
Relative to conventionally annealed steel, short-range-ordered steel will have a lower corrosion rate.
Relative to conventionally annealed steel, short-range-ordered steel will develop fewer pit-initiation sites.
Relative to conventionally annealed steel, short-range-ordered steel will exhibit improved long-term passivity.
Standard stainless-steel processing produces a less uniformly protective passive film and consequently a higher corrosion rate than the specialized treatment.
The proposed effect is expected to apply to steels containing at least about 12% chromium.
High impurity levels or substantial mechanical damage that disrupts the passive film may eliminate the benefit of short-range ordering.
Grain-boundary character, residual stress, and inclusions could contribute to observed corrosion resistance independently of short-range ordering.
A 3.5% NaCl solution and potentiodynamic testing can be used to investigate corrosion behavior.
Potentiodynamic polarization curves can quantify corrosion rates.

The hypothesis would be falsified if the treated steel showed no statistically significant improvement, or performed worse, in corrosion rate, pit density, and passive-film integrity relative to the untreated control.
